summary: Revises the IANA registration guidelines and procedures for Enumservices, which describe services associated with telephone numbers in ENUM, and gives a guide for writing Enumservice specifications. It is a proposed standard and obsoletes RFC 3761.

eli5.summary: The rules for adding new entries to an official list of services you can reach through a phone number, including a form to fill out.

questions: what is specification required in iana
subtitle: How to define and register an Enumservice, the label that says what a phone number's DNS record points to.

tldr.problem: Enumservice specifications varied too much in format, and the old registration rules from RFC 3761 were tied to the ENUM working group and to standards-track or experimental RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6117 requires only Specification Required with a Designated Expert, sets naming rules and classes for Enumservices, lists the sections every specification must contain, and defines an XML registration template and a seven-step process.
tldr.outcome: Anyone can follow a clear path to register an Enumservice, and experts check each request against published criteria. The RFC obsoletes Section 3 of RFC 3761.

today: RFC 6117 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2011. It obsoletes Section 3 of RFC 3761, and no RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Enumservices and What Changed
sections.content:
E.164 Number Mapping (ENUM) uses the Domain Name System to map phone numbers to URIs. One primary concept of ENUM is the Enumservice, which allows different URIs to be given for different applications of that mapping. An Enumservice is made up of a Type and, optionally, a Subtype.

RFC 6117 revises the IANA registry for Enumservices originally described in RFC 3761. It obsoletes Section 3 of RFC 3761, while RFC 6116 obsoletes RFC 3761 as a whole. The new processes are designed to be decoupled from the existence of the ENUM working group.

The main changes: registration now needs only "Specification Required" (which implies a Designated Expert) under RFC 5226, and the template gains elements for Enumservice Class and Enumservice Specification.
sections.eli5: An Enumservice is a label on a phone-number entry that says what you can do with it. This RFC changes how new labels get approved and makes the write-ups more alike.

sections.title: Registration Requirements
sections.content:
A complete Enumservice Specification MUST document the semantics of the Type and Subtype values and contain all sections listed in Section 5 of the RFC. The registered Enumservice must work as a selection mechanism for choosing one NAPTR DNS record from a set, so the specification must say how the NAPTR and its URIs are used and which URI schemes apply.

Naming rules: the Type must be unique, and a Subtype must be unique within its Type. Both must follow the ABNF in RFC 6116, are case insensitive and SHOULD be written in lowercase. A dash MUST NOT be the first, second or last character, and neither may start with e2u.

Security analysis is required for every Enumservice. A statement of "no security issues" must not be confused with "not assessed", and all known risks must be identified. Specifications must be published under "Specification Required"; publishing as an RFC is strongly RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A new label needs a unique name, a clear explanation of how it works, and a check for dangers. The name cannot be confusing, and it should be written in small letters.

sections.title: Classes of Enumservice
sections.content:
The RFC classifies Enumservices and gives advice on choosing Type and Subtype strings for each class. The classification must be listed in the registration document; if none fits, the document must explain the difficulty.

  • Protocol-Based: interaction uses the named protocol, such as xmpp or sip. The Type SHOULD be the lowercase protocol name.
  • Application-Based, in three cases. Common: a kind of interaction that different protocols can realize, such as email or SMS. Subset: a subset of what a protocol can do, such as voice:tel and fax:tel. Ancillary: further processing is the intended result, such as pstn:tel for number portability data.
  • Data Type-Based: refers to a data format, such as vpim and vcard.
  • Other: used when none fits, with a section explaining why.

A URI scheme name MUST NOT be used as a Type for an Enumservice that is not about that protocol. The RFC's example is that imap would be wrong for an "Internet mapping" service.
sections.eli5: Labels come in kinds: ones named after a tool (like a phone call method), ones named after a task (like email), and ones named after a file type (like a contact card).

sections.title: Required Sections and the Registration Template
sections.content:
An Enumservice Specification SHOULD contain, in order: Introduction, IANA Registration, Examples, optional Implementation Notes, DNS Considerations, Security Considerations and IANA Considerations. Other sections are optional, but a use case SHOULD be included to help the experts.

The IANA Registration section uses an XML chunk with these elements: class, type, subtype, urischeme, functionalspec, security, usage, registrationdocs, requesters and additionalinfo. If a Type has several Subtypes, each needs its own registration section. The usage value is one of COMMON, LIMITED USE or DEPRECATED.

DNS Considerations must cover issues such as use of wildcards, additional load on name servers and mitigation of DNS loops, particularly for Enumservices that use the tel URI scheme. Examples must show at least one NAPTR record plus a plain-English explanation.
sections.eli5: The form has fixed boxes: what kind it is, its name, which kinds of links it uses, what it does, and who asked for it. You also have to write what could go wrong.

sections.title: The Registration Process
sections.content:
The RFC describes a non-normative seven-step path; the normative process is in RFC 5226.

  1. Read the RFC in detail.
  2. Write the Registration Document and make it public.
  3. Ask for comments by emailing enum@ietf.org, allowing a reasonable period such as two to four weeks. Depending on feedback, authors submit no changes, minor changes, or substantial changes and ask again.
  4. Submit the document to IANA for Expert Review.
  5. The experts approve, require changes or reject it.
  6. The authors publish the document according to "Specification Required".
  7. The Enumservice is added to the IANA registry.

If published as an RFC, the RFC publication process ensures IANA adds the entry. For a non-RFC specification, the authors must tell IANA and provide a stable URL, and IANA keeps an escrow copy that acts as the master reference.
sections.eli5: You write your idea down, ask people what they think, hand it to the checkers, publish it, and then it goes on the official list.

sections.title: Expert Review and Change Control
sections.content:
Experts are appointed by the IESG. They follow RFC 5226, which stays authoritative if there is a conflict, and should also check conformance with RFC 6116 and the requirements of this document, whether the proposal matches its use case and whether an existing Enumservice already covers it, and that it cannot be confused with a similar entry. They look for negative side effects on clients and DNS, and for query loops when the output (especially a tel URI) could feed more ENUM processing.

IANA checks for earlier requests with an identical type:subtype and may reject a request if the published version differs substantially from the approved one. Change control follows the same process as initial registration, and the change controllers are the experts and the IESG. Registrations must not be deleted; an obsolete Enumservice is marked DEPRECATED.

Existing specifications MAY be revised to comply with this document. Adding a Subtype without other changes calls for an update, while a change to the default or to client URI assumptions needs a replacement.
sections.eli5: The checkers look for copies, muddle and trouble for the internet. Once a label is on the list it is never erased; it is only marked as old.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 6117 introduces no new technology, protocol or Enumservice, so it has no specific security issues of its own. It is a guide for authors, and the security guidance for authors and experts is in its Section 5.6.

That guidance says a specification must describe threats particular to the registration, including access to personally identifiable information. It should not repeat the considerations already in RFC 6116 or those of the underlying protocols, but should cover new issues that arise from including them in ENUM. Risks the RFC lists include directives that cause unrestricted actions, information disclosure that violates privacy, and applications that need security assurances the Enumservice cannot provide.
sections.eli5: This instruction sheet is not dangerous itself, but it tells authors to think about how a new label could be misused or leak private information.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3761
sections.content:
Compared with RFC 3761, which required Standards Track or Experimental RFCs, this document mandates "Specification Required" with a Designated Expert. It adds classification of Enumservices and a class element, adds the registrationdocs element, and renames the old free-form "any other information" field to additionalinfo.

The Enumservice "Name" field is removed, and the template becomes a chunk of XML data, reflecting IANA's conversion of registries to XML. The existing Enumservices were transformed into the new template by RFC 6118.
sections.eli5: The old rules were stricter about who could add labels. The new form is simpler to approve and is written in a computer-friendly format.

items.label: Named protocol
items.desc: Interaction uses the protocol, e.g. xmpp or sip.

items.label: Common application
items.desc: A kind of interaction different protocols can realize, e.g. email.

items.label: Subset
items.desc: A subset of what a protocol can do, e.g. voice:tel.

items.label: Ancillary
items.desc: Further processing is the result, e.g. pstn:tel.

items.label: Data format
items.desc: Refers to a data format, e.g. vcard.

items.label: Other
items.desc: Fits none of the classes; the specification explains why.
